title: People turn again
hook: human life shrinks, then people turn back to goodness; Metteyya will come

segments.voice: Yesterday: a king who stopped sharing, and your line, poverty breeds violence. What did you give? Today the same story hits bottom, and then something turns. Day five hundred fifty-nine.

The Cakkavatti Sihanada keeps going down. With every new kind of wrongdoing, the story says, human lifespans shrink, from tens of thousands of years down and down, until people live just ten years. Fine foods disappear. The very idea of a good deed disappears; there's not even a word for good. People treat each other like animals. And then comes something the text calls a sword-interval: seven days in which people see each other as prey, and kill. It's as dark as anything in the canon. And it isn't the end. Today: people turn again.
screen: `LIFE SHRINKS TO TEN YEARS.` → `NO WORD FOR GOOD.` → `SEVEN DAYS OF SWORDS.`

segments.voice: During those seven days, some people slip away. They hide in long grass, in thickets, in forests, among rocks and rivers, living on roots and fruit. When the seven days are over, they come out. And they see each other, and they embrace. The story gives their words simply: how good to see living beings still alive! Then they talk. We lost so much because we took up wrong ways. What if we gave up just one thing? What if we stopped killing? And they do. Just that one. And their children live a little longer. Seeing this, they give up something else: taking what isn't given. Then lying. Then harsh speech. Step by step, each generation adds one good thing, and human life lengthens again, all the way back to eighty thousand years. Then, the Buddha says, a Buddha named Metteyya will arise in the world, as I have arisen now, and he will teach the same Dhamma, good in the beginning, the middle and the end, and lead a community of many thousands, as I lead hundreds. Two things stand out. First, the turn starts with one small change, made by frightened people who are simply glad to see each other alive. Not a hero, not a king. Second, the hope is long. Many Buddhists in many lands look forward to Metteyya, known in Sanskrit as Maitreya, the Buddha to come. Metteyya's name is often linked with metta, loving-kindness. After all that darkness, the future has a kind name.
screen: `THE ONES WHO HID.` · `HOW GOOD TO SEE YOU ALIVE.` · `ONE GOOD THING AT A TIME.` · `METTEYYA WILL COME.` · then, large: `PEOPLE TURN AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the picture of the survivors come: people stepping out of the forest, seeing each other, glad. Breathe with that gladness. Then look forward, not with worry but with hope. Picture one good change that could spread, one generation adding one thing. Maybe it's something you could start. Rest with that future for a while. The bell holds the time.
People turn again. In DN 26, after the worst, survivors give up killing, then one wrong after another, and life grows long until Metteyya comes. Today's word.
Your line: people turn again. Today, when the news is bleak, look for one small good change someone is making, and be glad of it. Day five hundred fifty-nine.

howItsDone: Buddhists across Asia honor Metteyya, or Maitreya, as the coming Buddha, often depicted seated with feet on the ground, ready to rise, and many make merit in the hope of meeting his teaching.

fork.setup: you've survived seven days of violence by hiding in the forest. you come out and meet other survivors. what happens?
options: you embrace, glad they're alive, and agree to stop killing.
you go back into hiding for good.
fork.reveal: they embrace, say how good it is to see living beings, and give up killing. one good change starts the turn.

original.note: Pali Metteyya (Sanskrit Maitreya): the Buddha to come, named in DN 26. the name is often linked with metta, loving-kindness.

trapdoor: what you thought: Buddhist time only goes downhill.
what it means: in DN 26 life sinks to its worst, then people turn back, one good thing at a time.
what a scholar hears: DN 26 is one of very few early Pali suttas to name Metteyya; the later Maitreya traditions across Asia grew from small seeds like this.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 26 (Cakkavatti Sihanada Sutta), the sword-interval, the return to goodness and Metteyya

notes: DN 26 paraphrased. Confirm the ten-year lifespan, the absence of a word for 'good' (kusala), the seven-day sattha-antara-kappa, and the survivors' words.
Confirm the order of what is given up after killing, and the rise back to eighty thousand years.
Confirm DN 26 is one of very few early Nikaya passages naming Metteyya, and the 'thousands vs hundreds' line.
The link of Metteyya with metta is a common gloss; confirm framing.
